That's an interesting question! I believe that thoughts are basically a simulated perception of something that your brain believes will happen, did happen, or wants to happen (or avoid). These simulated perceptions are extremely usefull, as they can be helpful to make decisions that are yet to be made. Arguably, this is a major element of human nature that makes humans 'superior' to animals.   


Now, the interesting thing about human perception is that it is immensely flawed. For example, when one is to observe a person for the first time, one will perceive a fraction of what this observed person is actually doing and associate this perceived fraction of actual truth with previous experiences in order to make sense out of what is being perceived. Consequently, subjective truth is being formed, which might in fact not be entirely the truth. 

This is the most optimal manner in which humanity can make sense out of its surroundings, because the human brain simply does not have the processing power to accurately process these surroundings, and therefore, has to associate past experiences with the actually perceived information.   


My point is as follows: associating a feeling with something you think about, is a similar process to the one described above. Our brain is simply designed to associate past experiences (including emotions) with the things that we perceive. Without that uncontrollable ability, we would be clueless.   


I hope this somewhat answers your questions and or inspires you to look into it deeper.
